A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BARBAT framework and its extensions. The main text, algorithms, mathematical material and appendices support comparison. The proofs can be matched across their extensive reordering.

before.justification: v1 reports algorithms, theoretical regret comparisons and proofs, including Appendices A–E, but no original empirical results.

after.justification: v2 Section 5 and Appendix C report original synthetic bandit experiments, regret curves and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The core BARBAT framework is retained. BB-BARBAT removes the lower clamp of 2 on its growth parameter a. OODS also corrects its loop condition from continuing while the graph is empty to continuing while it is not empty (v1 Algorithm 3; v2 Algorithm 6). These are localized procedural changes.

E1.justification: v1 covers the bandit settings theoretically without empirical evaluation. v2 adds actual synthetic evaluations of cooperative multi-agent bandits, strongly observable graph bandits with two directed feedback graphs, and d-set semi-bandits. Batched bandits remain without empirical evaluation.

E2.justification: v2 introduces empirical comparisons absent from v1: DRAA, IND-BARBAR and IND-FTRL for multi-agent bandits; Shannon-FTRL and Tsallis-FTRL for graph bandits; and HYBRID, LBINF, LBINF_LS and LBINF_GD for semi-bandits. Their participation is confirmed in Figures 1–3. Elise is explicitly excluded from the graph experiments.

E3.justification: The new experiments introduce protocols using T = 50000, K = 12 or 16, and corruption budgets C = 2000 or 5000. Multi-agent experiments use V = 10; semi-bandits use d = 3 or 4. Appendix C specifies reward generation and an attack favoring the two worst arms. Regret and runtime are evaluated.

E4.justification: Figures 1–3 add limited corruption-budget sensitivity checks by comparing C = 2000 and 5000. Section 5.1 specifically examines how individual regret increases with corruption. v1 contains no corresponding empirical analysis; v2 does not add component ablations or comparisons across different attack families.

E5.justification: v1 has no empirical repeated-run or uncertainty reporting. v2 Section 5 specifies 50 independent trials, reports averages, and identifies the shaded regions in Figures 1–3 as standard deviations. This introduces uncertainty reporting throughout the new empirical evaluation; seed values and significance tests are not supplied.

E6.justification: v2 adds all empirical results in Figures 1–3 and Tables 2–3, with no corresponding measurements in v1. The curves show lower regret for the BARBAT variants than their tested comparators. Table 3 reports, for example, 0.36 seconds for BARBAT versus 14.63 seconds for HYBRID at K = 12. These are newly reported comparisons.

T1.justification: The principal regret guarantees are largely retained. v2 reworks the domination-set proof from v1 Lemma 12 into Lemma 24 using Turan's theorem and a separate undirected-graph argument, and changes the graph theorem's cardinality bound from floor to ceiling. It also corrects the main-text semi-bandit gap sign and changes the batched epoch-count lemma to M = L.

C1.justification: The central claims about removing the multiplicative corruption factor K, near-optimal regret and scalable extensions remain. v2 qualifies the introduction's computational comparison with FTRL by explicitly recognizing Shannon-entropy regularization's closed-form exception. The new experiments primarily support existing efficiency and robustness claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of the empirical comparisons as evidence for collaboration and lower sensitivity to corruption, and argues that regret against true means is more natural than regret against corrupted rewards. Existing qualifications concerning the batched upper/lower-bound gap, communication with multiple optimal arms, and logarithmic regret factors remain.

D1.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C add substantial experimental documentation absent from v1: Python 3.11, Windows, an Intel i7-13700H processor, 16 GB memory, reward distributions, corruption construction and feedback-graph generation parameters. These support reproduction of the new experiments, although the PDF supplies no code-access link or detailed baseline solver settings.

R1.justification: The overall positioning against BARBAR and FTRL remains. Table 1 revises the treatment of efficient Shannon-FTRL and changes the cited CBARAC corruption term from VC to C. The Ito et al. (2024) graph comparison is removed, while references supporting Turan's theorem and random-graph generation are added.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: task definitions are consolidated in Section 2, the introductory technique discussion moves into Section 3 with a worked example, and the extensions are reordered. OODS receives Appendix A, proofs are consolidated under Appendix B, and an appendix contents page is added. The title and substantial explanatory prose are also revised.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands and restructures Table 1, including lower-bound rows and explicit method names. It adds three multi-panel regret figures, a feedback-graph diagram and two runtime tables. Algorithm blocks are restyled and relocated, including moving OODS into the appendix. These are substantial display and layout changes.

improvement.justification: The repeated-trial regret comparisons and runtime tables provide useful empirical support for efficiency and robustness claims previously supported only theoretically, and the reorganization improves accessibility. However, the experiments cover limited synthetic settings, and BB-BARBAT introduces an inconsistency: Algorithm 3 removes the clamp on a while Appendix B.3 still uses the clamped definition and assumes a >= 2. These limitations temper the evidential and presentation gains.
